source.title: Adaptive Inertia: Disentangling the Effects of Adaptive Learning Rate and Momentum
source.authors: Zeke Xie; Xin-Rui Wang; Hui-Shuai Zhang; Issei Sato; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: Full paper text is supplied, including appendices. Some table formatting is flattened, and the CIFAR-100 portion of Table 2 has no results in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares test performance across optimizers, a different empirical method aimed at the optimizer-generalization claim. It does not test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: Table 2 and Figures 2–4 and 13 report the paper's optimizer comparisons. The text also cites prior optimizer results, which are not recorded as rows. Figure-only learning curves are omitted where the text does not report a usable value.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares optimizers using held-out image-classification error and language-model perplexity, the same method and measures used to test V4. It is not an original source for V4. CIFAR comparisons favor SGD in learning-rate tuning effort; ImageNet and Penn TreeBank use learning-rate searches for each optimizer.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: under their diffusion assumptions, adaptive learning rates weaken flat-minimum selection relative to SGD, whereas momentum preserves it; Adai combines faster saddle escape with favorable minima selection. They report generally better empirical generalization for Adai, although on Penn TreeBank it ties Adam at 74.3 perplexity.
record.recipe_differences: Compares optimizers on standard image and language tasks, but does not test the original cited studies' full benchmark suite or controlled limited-tuning setup. Learning-rate selection differs between non-adaptive and adaptive methods; explicit weight decay is used in the image experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and task affect the Adam-versus-SGD result: Adam has higher test error on the reported image-classification comparisons, but lower test perplexity than SGD Momentum on Penn TreeBank.

fits_no_version.finding: The diffusion analysis and Figure 6 compare optimizer escape times as minima curvature changes; Figures 7 and 14 compare Hessian eigenvalues and sensitivity to Gaussian weight noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam selects sharper minima than momentum SGD under the studied dynamics and experiments. These results do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of generalization gaps.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning; PMLR 162, 2022)
record.problems: Optimizer tuning is not matched: for CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, the paper selects learning rates for non-adaptive methods but uses the original papers' default learning rates for adaptive methods. Table values are flattened, obscuring exact mean/standard-deviation formatting. The supplied Table 2 text has no recoverable CIFAR-100 result values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the reported explicit numerical Adam-versus-SGD comparisons. Figure-only learning curves in Figures 2, 3, 11, and 13 were not extracted as separate rows where no exact value is stated in text; explicit values from Figure 13 and Figure 4 are included.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label held-out generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.

Whether broader hyperparameter tuning removes or reverses the Adam–SGD difference; switching from Adam to SGD. Equal or better Adam training performance is not established numerically by the extracted rows.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and remedies for large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions; the language model uses fixed dropout without an ablation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps and comparative ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence and retraining.

missing.what: Other adaptive-method comparisons in Table 2, particularly AdamW's reduced gaps, Padam's VGG16 advantage (6.15 ± 0.06% versus SGD 6.42 ± 0.02%), and AdaBelief's near-SGD results on several models. These qualify how broadly the adaptive-method disadvantage holds.

Table 3 supplies additional explicit comparisons at weight decay 0.0001. Adam errors are 6.08, 7.04, 25.56, 24.39, 24.60%, versus matched SGD errors 5.58, 6.92, 24.92, 20.98, 21.89%. AdamW beats this SGD baseline on ResNet18, VGG16, ResNet34 and GoogLeNet, but remains worse on DenseNet121. Record these separately from the repeated stronger SGD reference columns.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains recoverable CIFAR-100 values; the record's claim that these are missing is incorrect. The study tests only V4. Its language-model result supports an explicit qualification of V4 rather than challenging it. CIFAR tuning asymmetry limits attribution of the observed differences to optimizer choice alone.

versions.untested_parts: Limited-tuning comparison on the stated image-classification and language benchmarks in general; learning-rate and decay tuning are not matched across methods in all experiments; broader tuning and switching from Adam to SGD are not tested.
Large-batch versus small-batch performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of training-test gap across similarly low-training-loss networks.
